title: Australia’s AI investment boom arrives before the productivity dividend
summary: For Australia, the first measurable effects of artificial intelligence may appear in investment, equipment imports and pressure on skilled trades well before they show up in output per hour. Assistant Governor Sarah Hunter set out this timing problem using the supply and demand channels in Figure 1. Published estimates of how AI could change annual productivity growth over the next decade range from 0.1 per cent to more than 2 per cent a year in the studies she cited. The range reflects how much depends on adoption, the reorganisation of work and the creation of new products. In the meantime, the infrastructure needed for AI already draws on labour, electricity and capital.

The adoption figures show how much can happen inside firms before the aggregate measure moves. Among the RBA’s liaison respondents, the share reporting no AI use fell from 32 per cent in 2025 to less than 1 per cent in 2026. Yet 60 per cent reported only limited adoption in 2026, and roughly 10 per cent reported deep or transformative use. On a separate productivity question, 36 per cent reported no gains yet, compared with 12 per cent reporting significant gains. These are responses from business contacts. The survey does not weight a minute saved on a single task by the task’s share of national output. Reorganising workflows, training staff and checking output take resources before widespread gains can show up in GDP. Graph 1 compares different liaison samples, question wording and fieldwork windows. The 2025 interviews ran from May to August and the 2026 interviews from June to October. The change in the bars describes the two groups interviewed. It does not track a fixed group of firms as they moved from one stage of adoption to the next.

Hunter’s estimate of realised Australian data-centre investment had increased tenfold in three years from a very low base. The size of the order for a data centre and the addition to domestic income are different quantities. Many servers are imported. Local demand is more concentrated in construction, engineering, electricity generation and transmission, including trades that liaison contacts already regarded as stretched. Overseas, equipment exports from Taiwan and South Korea illustrate who can receive the corresponding manufacturing orders. In a forecaster’s accounts, recording gross investment without the associated imports overstates the direct contribution to Australian GDP. Applying the same import share to electricians and grid connections would understate local pressure. Graph 3 puts forecast spending by large technology companies for 2026 and 2027 on the left axis and machinery and equipment exports from Taiwan and South Korea on a separate axis. Only the lighter spending bars are Bloomberg forecasts. Graph 4 switches to Australian quarterly investment volumes. The data-centre series is an RBA estimate inferred from telecommunications and information-media capital expenditure. Its separate dot is a November nowcast informed by trade and spending intentions. A project announcement, an imported server arriving at a port and a completed centre contributing to domestic output can fall in different quarters.

The inflation comparison across Australia, Canada, the United Kingdom and the United States shows rapidly rising prices in some electronics categories. Their CPI weights are small. Repeated price and wage pressure in construction or electricity would be stronger evidence of transmission beyond those products. Further ahead, additional capacity could relieve bottlenecks as productivity improves. That prospect does not establish a persistent negative inflation impulse: households could spend more as their incomes rise, and a global investment boom could increase demand for savings. Hunter described the possible rise in the neutral interest rate as difficult to quantify. A rise in a bond yield alone cannot distinguish stronger capital demand from a change in risk compensation.

Hunter also considered whether strong investment demand could lift the global rate that balances saving and investment, especially if households brought consumption forward against higher expected incomes. Graph 6 shows the Australian nominal cash rate against an average of neutral-rate models. Its shaded band covers the range of central estimates, leaving additional uncertainty within each model. Market-based estimates run to September 2026 and the other models to June. Hunter reported that market participants had cited demand for capital as a reason bond yields had risen. Neither the chart nor that attribution isolates how much AI moved the neutral rate. A higher observed bond yield alone gives no measure of how much more or less restrictive the cash rate had become.

Household wealth introduces a route in both directions. Staff put exposure to AI-related equities at about 5 per cent of Australian household financial wealth, including holdings through superannuation. A valuation gain inside a retirement account need not produce the same consumption response as an increase in disposable income. Employment was similarly uneven. Roughly three quarters of liaison respondents reported no headcount effect. Among the remainder, slower hiring was more common than reducing existing staff. Younger workers in highly exposed occupations showed some relative weakness in advertising and employment, but the underlying differences were modest. Jobs and Skills Australia’s 4 per cent highly exposed to automation and 31 per cent highly exposed to augmentation describe the tasks in jobs. They give no direct estimate of jobs likely to disappear. Graph 9 measures annual growth in new job advertisements. Graph 10 instead indexes employment to November 2022 and separates workers aged 15–24 from those aged 25–64. An employer can reduce vacancies while retaining staff, so the two series need not fall together. Graph 11 measures potential exposure at the occupation level. Hunter reported that about 4% of Australian workers were highly exposed to automation and 31% to augmentation. Those shares measure the tasks technology could affect. They do not give the proportions who had lost jobs or received pay increases.

questions.question: How much Australian demand does a dollar of announced data-centre investment create, and when?
questions.detail: Break projects into imported equipment, site and building works, electrical installation, network connections and ongoing operation. Match goods arrivals to completed construction and paid local labour rather than treating the value of announced projects as immediate activity. Tracking announced, commenced and completed projects separately would help locate the peak pressure on domestic labour and materials.

questions.question: What evidence would justify a higher estimate of trend productivity growth?
questions.detail: Follow output per hour, adoption depth and implementation costs across consecutive quarters in similar industries. Demand that shifts toward more productive firms can improve a sector average without improving any given firm. A sustained increase after deployment within several industries would be more persuasive than a higher count of firms reporting some use.

questions.question: Where is the marginal inflation risk visible outside computer equipment?
questions.detail: Apply actual CPI weights to changes in consumer electronics prices, then compare construction wages, engineering vacancies, network investment and electricity costs in areas with substantial data-centre work. Distinguish demand arriving from other infrastructure projects. This would reveal whether the price effect remains inside a narrow basket or is competing away capacity elsewhere.

questions.question: Are employers reducing entry-level opportunities while keeping total employment steady?
questions.detail: Compare new hires, vacancies and employment for younger and established workers within similar occupations. Allow for the post-pandemic hiring cycle and other demand changes in technology-intensive firms. If advertised junior roles fall while experienced workers remain employed and productive, aggregate headcount would miss a loss of entry routes and the associated longer-run training costs.
